name: tree-pattern-matcher
intent: Separate the subtree shapes an analysis or a rewrite cares about from the traversal that finds them, so rules are stated as pattern/action pairs over the tree while an engine owns walking, matching and rewriting - term rewriting instead of a hand-written visitor.
problem: A pass over a syntax tree or IR must react to particular subtree shapes - x + 0, an assignment whose right-hand side is a call, the expression subtrees inside a statement - but those shapes do not line up with node types. Written as a plain visitor, the structure test and the action share visit methods, every analysis re-implements the walk, shape knowledge is spread over several methods, and unrelated syntax cannot be skipped cheaply; what the code actually needs is dispatch on structure rather than on nominal node type.
context: Compiler front and middle ends, analyzers, linters, refactoring and codemod tools, and language servers: a stable tree (AST, IR, parse tree or CST) is traversed by several tasks, the shapes of interest are sparse relative to the tree, and either the toolchain already ships a matcher engine (ANTLR parse tree patterns, clang AST matchers, Roslyn rewriters, NodePattern, ESLint selectors, tree-sitter queries, syn's fold) or the team is willing to build a small rule engine over its own node types.
benefits: Rules are declarative data: the subtree shapes of interest and their actions are stated once, reviewed as a table, and tested in isolation with tree fixtures.
The traversal is written once and reused: adding an analysis or a rewrite adds a rule, not another walk, and a single pass can try many patterns.

Unrelated syntax is skipped by construction - only the shapes you specify are matched - so rules stay short instead of enumerating node kinds nobody cares about (the awk, sed and perl analogy Parr draws).

Dispatch follows structure rather than nominal type: a pattern can span node kinds and constrain children, which avoids the double dispatch and visitor-side shape tests that type-based dispatch needs.
Rewrites are pattern-to-replacement pairs, so peephole optimisation, algebraic simplification, instruction selection and source codemods all share one mechanism.
Captures make the action's inputs explicit: the matched parts the action needs are named and bound (bind, $, tags, labels), which keeps actions small and honest about what they depend on.
Coverage can be measured: an engine can report matched versus visited nodes, so gaps in the rule set become visible instead of hiding in unimplemented visit methods.
tradeoffs: The rule set is a second language with its own ordering and precedence semantics: two rules that both match produce order-dependent results, and nothing in the pattern notation expresses which one must win unless the engine defines it.
Non-matching is silent by design: a rule set complete enough for today's task skips unhandled shapes without warning, so the source cannot show which tree shapes are unanalysed.

Structural patterns cannot see context: the same node shape occurs in positions with different meanings (an isolated identifier versus an identifier inside an array index), so rules need root restrictions or guards, and full context needs a tree grammar or a symbol-aware pass.

Cost multiplies with rules: every node may be tried against every pattern unless the engine indexes patterns by root kind, so a naive engine turns many rules into repeated walks or near-quadratic matching.

Rewriting during the walk makes ordering and termination the engine's job: a rule that rewrites to a shape it still matches loops, and a rewrite applied twice is not idempotent in general - control flow a hand-written pass would state explicitly.

Bindings are checked dynamically, or parsed from strings: a rule that matches the wrong nodes compiles (or parses) and fails only when the captured nodes are used, which is why ANTLR patterns need precise labels and scalameta warns about quasiquote patterns.
Debugging a misfire spans three things at once - the pattern, the engine's traversal and application policy, and the actual tree shape - whereas a visitor's bug lives in one function.

participants.responsibility: The AST, IR, parse tree or CST being analysed or rewritten; a matcher engine needs the tree to expose node kinds, children and, for rewrites, stable identity or source positions.
A subtree shape: a node kind plus constraints on named children, with wildcards and quantifiers for the parts the rule does not care about - the unit the engine tries at each node.
A hole in the pattern that binds the matched node or node sequence (bind, $, tags, labels) so the action can address exactly the parts of the match it needs.
What happens on a match: annotate the node with computed information, or produce a replacement subtree or source edit; in rewriting systems the action is itself a pattern-to-pattern mapping.
The ordered collection of pattern/action pairs plus guards (semantic predicates), together with the precedence and application policy the engine follows.
Owns traversal and application strategy - top-down or bottom-up, once or repeatedly until a fixpoint, which subtrees to skip, how patterns are indexed - so that no rule contains traversal code.

use_cases: Peephole and algebraic rewriting in a middle end: simplification rules such as x + 0 -> x, !true -> false or a * 1 -> a, applied bottom-up to a fixpoint.

Instruction selection and IR canonicalisation, where the target instruction is chosen by matching operand patterns over a DAG or over instructions (TableGen ISel patterns, LLVM PatternMatch in InstCombine).
Codemods and refactoring tools: find-and-rewrite rules over a real source tree (rename, remove, modernise syntax) where only the interesting subtrees should be touched.
Semantic analysis that annotates expressions - Parr's Cymbol type computation matches EXPR roots and invokes a separate rule on the expression subtree, storing evalType on the matched node.
Lint and policy rules expressed as guarded subtree patterns (no-restricted-syntax selectors, RuboCop node patterns, clang-tidy matchers) that report or autocorrect the matched shape.
Editor and language-server queries: tree-sitter query files that capture nodes for highlighting, folding, injection and structural navigation without writing a walker.

.NET refactorings and code fixes as Roslyn syntax rewriters: the official syntax-transformation guide subclasses CSharpSyntaxRewriter, overrides the Visit method for the declaration shape it cares about (LocalDeclarationStatementSyntax) and returns a replacement node, pairing the syntactic pattern with a SemanticModel check for the context the pattern cannot see.

Rust procedural macros and codemods rewriting owned syntax trees with syn's Fold trait: overriding one hook (e.g. fold_expr) rewrites every matching expression - the documented use is replacing panic! invocations or parenthesising expressions - and because fold returns rebuilt nodes, the input tree is never mutated under the walker.
avoid_when: Only one node type needs a small structural check: a recursive function, a match expression or a single visit method is simpler than an engine plus a rule notation.

The rule needs context the pattern cannot see (enclosing scope, types, declaration site): a symbol-aware pass, a tree grammar or a visitor carrying that context is the honest tool - Parr's type-computation example needs the EXPR-root restriction for exactly this reason.

The check must be exhaustive over every node kind (a verifier that has to visit everything): a tree grammar or a compiler-checked match makes completeness visible, while a pattern set silently skips unlisted shapes.
A mature tool already implements the rule you need (clang-tidy check, ESLint rule, Roslyn analyzer, RuboCop cop): configure or extend it instead of building a second matcher over the same tree.

The rewrite must be applied exactly once, or provably idempotent under tight control: a hand-written pass states the control flow and the termination argument explicitly, where a repeated-application engine leaves both implicit.
anti_patterns: Encoding an entire tree grammar as a bag of patterns: the set is invisible and incomplete, so nobody can tell which tree shapes are unhandled - the very gap between Parr's Tree Grammar and Tree Pattern Matcher.
Mutating the tree while the matcher walks it, so rules fire on nodes that no longer exist or fire twice depending on traversal order.
Wildcards so broad that a rule fires on semantically different subtrees, then guards and negations piled on until the pattern no longer reads like the shape it matches.
Near-duplicate patterns per node kind where one rule with captured children (or one rule indexed by root kind) would do - the combinator explosion that makes a rule set unmaintainable.
Treating a clean run as evidence of a clean tree: a report of zero findings is indistinguishable from a rule set that never fired on the relevant syntax.

Rebuilding a matcher over a framework that already ships one - a hand-rolled ESTree walker next to ESLint, a custom Clang matcher next to clang-tidy, a bespoke PSI walk next to an existing inspection.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: what to match and what to do are declared independently of how the tree is walked.
Declarative rules over imperative traversal: shape knowledge is data the engine interprets, not control flow distributed across visit methods.
Open/closed principle: a new analysis or rewrite is a new rule, not an edit to the walker or to the node classes.
Dispatch on structure, not nominal type: patterns span node kinds and constrain children, keeping shape-driven logic out of the type hierarchy.
Be explicit about what is ignored: wildcards and quantifiers document the parts of the tree a rule does not constrain, and guards document the context it assumes.

Completeness must be engineered, not assumed: because non-matches are silent, coverage needs its own evidence - matched versus visited counts, a fixture per pattern, an exhaustive grammar where required.
best_practices: Write one pattern per shape you actually care about and bind the parts the action uses; treat every wildcard as a deliberate statement that the rest of the subtree is irrelevant.
Decide and document the engine's strategy once: traversal order (top-down, bottom-up, both), application policy (once, repeated until stable), and the precedence between overlapping rules.
Never mutate the tree you are matching: annotate and rebuild in a later step, or rewrite a copy, so every rule sees the structure its pattern was written against.
Prove termination for rewriting rule sets: no rule may rewrite to a shape that it, or a later rule, matches again, and repeated application must be bounded explicitly.
Keep rules small and guarded: prefer captured children plus a predicate over a pattern that enumerates structure only to discard it.
Track coverage: count matched versus visited nodes, log interesting shapes that matched nothing, and keep a positive plus a near-miss fixture for every pattern.
Reach for the ecosystem's matcher first (clang matchers, NodePattern, ESLint selectors, tree-sitter queries, syn fold, Roslyn rewriters) and build an engine only when the tree is your own.
sources: Parr, T., Language Implementation Patterns: Create Your Own Domain-Specific and General Programming Languages (Pragmatic Bookshelf, 2010) - Pattern 15, Tree Pattern Matcher (ch. 5, Walking and Rewriting Trees, p. 120), with Pattern 13 External Tree Visitor (p. 113), Pattern 14 Tree Grammar (p. 117) and section 5.4 Decoupling Tree Traversal from Pattern Matching (p. 108) as its immediate neighbours.

Parr, T., Language Implementation Patterns, Pattern 15 purpose - the pattern walks trees, triggering actions or tree rewrites as it encounters tree patterns of interest; matching and rewriting trees is formally term rewriting; unlike a tree grammar only the subtrees you care about are specified and the walk is not directed, making the matcher analogous to awk, sed and perl. https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/language-implementation-patterns/9781680500097/f_0057.html

Clang LibASTMatchers - a C++ DSL of composable predicates over the Clang AST with .bind() captures and an engine-owned traversal: the official matcher guide behind clang-tidy-style tools. https://clang.llvm.org/docs/LibASTMatchers.html

RuboCop NodePattern DSL - node-type sequences with repetition, alternation, $ captures and def_node_matcher macros, compiled to matching code over Parser AST nodes. https://docs.rubocop.org/rubocop-ast/latest/node_pattern.html

ESLint no-restricted-syntax - lint policy stated as ESTree selectors (e.g. CallExpression[callee.name='setTimeout'][arguments.length!=2]), with the docs' own advice to prefer simple selectors because complex ones add traversal cost - the cost note behind this pattern's performance tradeoff. https://eslint.org/docs/latest/rules/no-restricted-syntax
syn::fold - the Fold trait rewrites an owned Rust syntax tree hook by hook (fold_expr etc.), returning rebuilt nodes instead of mutating the tree. https://docs.rs/syn/latest/syn/fold/index.html

Roslyn syntax transformation - CSharpSyntaxRewriter walks the immutable C# syntax tree depth-first and replaces or removes nodes, combined with a SemanticModel for the context the syntactic pattern cannot see. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/roslyn-sdk/get-started/syntax-transformation
